entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen23536" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23537" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23538" type="x-p"/> The psalmist praises God for his goodness to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Psa.147.1-Psa.147.3">Psa 147:1-3</reference>; shows his great mercy to them that trust in him, <reference osisRef="Psa.147.4-Psa.147.6">Psa 147:4-6</reference>; he extols him for his mercies, and providential kindness, <reference osisRef="Psa.147.7-Psa.147.11">Psa 147:7-11</reference>; for his defense of Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Psa.147.12-Psa.147.15">Psa 147:12-15</reference>; For his wonders in the seasons, <reference osisRef="Psa.147.16-Psa.147.18">Psa 147:16-18</reference>; and his word unto Jacob, <reference osisRef="Psa.147.19">Psa 147:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.147.20">Psa 147:20</reference>. <div eID="gen23538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23539" type="x-p"/> This Psalm, which is without title in the Hebrew, Chaldee, and Vulgate, is attributed by the other Versions to Haggai and Zechariah. It was probably penned after the captivity, when the Jews were busily employed in rebuilding Jerusalem, as may be gathered from the second and thirteenth verses. It may be necessary to remark that all the Versions, except the Chaldee, divide this Psalm at the end of the eleventh verse, and begin a new Psalm at the twelfth. By this division the numbers of the Psalms agree in the Versions with the Hebrew; the former having been, till now, one behind. <div eID="gen23539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23540" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23541" type="x-p"/> Praise is comely - It is decent, befitting, and proper that every intelligent creature should acknowledge the Supreme Being: and as he does nothing but good to the children of men, so they should speak good of his name.
entries.content_plain: Introduction The psalmist praises God for his goodness to Jerusalem, Psa 147:1-3 ; shows his great mercy to them that trust in him, Psa 147:4-6 ; he extols him for his mercies, and providential kindness, Psa 147:7-11 ; for his defense of Jerusalem, Psa 147:12-15 ; For his wonders in the seasons, Psa 147:16-18 ; and his word unto Jacob, Psa 147:19 , Psa 147:20 . This Psalm, which is without title in the Hebrew, Chaldee, and Vulgate, is attributed by the other Versions to Haggai and Zechariah. It was probably penned after the captivity, when the Jews were busily employed in rebuilding Jerusalem, as may be gathered from the second and thirteenth verses. It may be necessary to remark that all the Versions, except the Chaldee, divide this Psalm at the end of the eleventh verse, and begin a new Psalm at the twelfth. By this division the numbers of the Psalms agree in the Versions with the Hebrew; the former having been, till now, one behind. Verse 1 Praise is comely - It is decent, befitting, and proper that every intelligent creature should acknowledge the Supreme Being: and as he does nothing but good to the children of men, so they should speak good of his name.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23543" type="x-p"/> He healeth the broken in heart - שבורי, the shivered in heart. From the root שבר shabar, to break in pieces, we have our word shiver, to break into splinters, into shivers. The heart broken in pieces by a sense of God's displeasure.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23548" type="x-p"/> Who covereth the heaven with clouds - Collects the vapours together, in order to cause it to rain upon the earth. Even the direction of the winds, the collection of the clouds, and the descent of the rain, are under the especial management of God. These things form a part of his providential management of the world. <div eID="gen23548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23549" type="x-p"/> Maketh grass to grow upon the mountains - After this clause the Vulgate, the Septuagint, Ethiopic, Arabic, and Anglo-Saxon, add, and herb for the service of man. It appears that a hemistich, or half-line, has been lost from the Hebrew text; which, according to the above Versions, must have stood thus: ועשב לעבדת האדם veeseb laabodath haadam, as in <reference osisRef="Psa.104.14">Psa 104:14</reference> : "And herbage for the service of mankind."

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen23549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23550" type="x-p"/> He delighteth not - The horse, among all animals, is most delighted in by man for beauty, strength, and fleetness. And a man's legs, if well proportioned, are more admired than even the finest features of his face. Though God has made these, yet they are not his peculiar delight.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen23550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23551" type="x-p"/> The Lord taketh pleasure in them that fear him - That are truly religious. <div eID="gen23551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23552" type="x-p"/> In those that hope is his mercy - Who are just beginning to seek the salvation of their souls. Even the cry of the penitent is pleasing in the ear of the Lord. With this verse the hundred and forty-sixth Psalm ends in all the Versions, except the Chaldee. And the hundred and forty-seventh commences with the <reference osisRef="Psa.147.12">Psa 147:12</reference>. I believe these to be two distinct Psalms. The subjects of them are not exactly the same, though something similar; and they plainly refer to different periods.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen23552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23553" type="x-p"/> He hath strengthened the bars of thy gates - He has enabled thee to complete the walls of Jerusalem. From the former part of the Psalm it appears the walls were then to progress; from this part, they appear to be completed, and provisions to be brought into the city, to support its inhabitants. The gates were set up and well secured by bars, so that the grain, etc., was in safety.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen23557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23558" type="x-p"/> He casteth forth his ice - קרחו korcho, (probably hailstones), like crumbs. <div eID="gen23558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23559" type="x-p"/> Who can stand before his cold? - At particular times the cold in the east is so very intense as to kill man and beast. Jacobus de Vitriaco, one of the writers in the Gesta Dei per Francos, says, that in an expedition in which he was engaged against Mount Tabor, on the 24th of December, the cold was so intense that many of the poor people, and the beasts of burden, died by it. And Albertus Aquensis, another of these writers, speaking of the cold in Judea, says, that thirty of the people who attended Baldwin 1: in the mountainous districts near the Dead Sea, were killed by it; and that in that expedition they had to contend with horrible hail and ice, with unheard-of snow and rain. From thls we find that the winters are often very severe in Judea; and in such cases as the above, we may well call out, "Who can stand against his cold!"
